section: 1.  Identify the most-recent date tag among saved CSVs
grain_in: one CSV file on disk in results/ whose name matches base_YYYY-MM-DD.csv
grain_out: one row per base name, holding the single file chosen for that base
operation: Builds a regex from the nine base names, lists results/, parses base and date out of each filename, keeps only the nine requested bases, then sorts by date and filename descending and takes the first row per base, so each base is represented by exactly one file; the tibble construction and the filename parsing are absorbed because they exist only to supply the sort keys. The missing-base warning at lines 113-116 is deliberately outside the region: it reports on this node but changes nothing. Note the selection is by the date written in the filename, not by file modification time, so a file relabelled with a later date wins.
settings: base_names: the nine fixed base names; regex requires a _YYYY-MM-DD.csv suffix; tie-break arrange(base, desc(date), desc(fname)) then slice_head(n = 1); results_dir fixed to script_dir/results
na_behavior: as.Date(str_extract(...)) would give NA for a filename without a date, but the regex filter makes that unreachable. A base with no matching file is silently dropped from the output and only produces a warning; the failure then surfaces later as a missing object at lines 143-151, where a missing file and a misspelled base name are indistinguishable.

section: 2. Read each latest file into a named list
inputs: e7_taylor.latest_file_per_base; INPUT:results/population_invariability_<date>.csv and the eight other selected CSVs
grain_in: one row per base name (a file path)
grain_out: one named list element per base, each holding that file's table at its own grain; for population_invariability the header block claims species x bay x season
units_out: whatever each file stores; for pop_inv, mu is a mean abundance and I_i an invariability index
operation: Reads each selected file with readr::read_csv and deframes path/table pairs into a named list, which is then attached to the global environment at line 140; the select and deframe are absorbed because they only reshape the container. Nothing checks that the file read is the file intended, and no column contract is asserted, so a schema change upstream enters here unnoticed. What one row of population_invariability represents cannot be determined from this script alone: the header comment says species x season x bay, but nothing here verifies that there is not also a period or year column.
settings: show_col_types = FALSE; readr default type guessing (guess_max = 1000 rows); no col_types contract; no explicit na argument, so the readr default set applies
na_behavior: Empty fields and the readr default NA strings become NA. Column-type guessing failures are not surfaced: problems() is never called, so a column that guessed wrong becomes silent NA. A value that was NA in the source file and a value that failed to parse are indistinguishable downstream.

grain_in: one population: species x bay x season (as documented in the file header, not verified in code)
grain_out: same grain, restricted to populations with finite mu and finite I_i
units_in: mu: mean abundance in the units of the source survey (per tow? per haul? not determinable from this script); I_i: dimensionless index
operation: Drops every row whose mu or I_i is not finite and overwrites pop_inv, so all later use of pop_inv sees the reduced set; this changes which populations the rest of the section describes. Removing non-finite I_i removes zero-variance populations in particular, since I_i = mu^2/sigma^2 is Inf when sigma^2 is 0, and those are exactly the perfectly stable populations. The rename at line 150 (pop_inv <- population_invariability) is not part of any node.
settings: is.finite applied to mu and I_i only; no threshold on sample size, series length, or number of observations behind each mean
na_behavior: NA, NaN, +Inf and -Inf are all removed by the same test, so a population absent from the survey, a population whose variance could not be computed, and a population with zero variance collapse into the same silent exclusion. The number of rows removed is never recorded or printed.

grain_in: one population: species x bay x season
grain_out: one fitted OLS line per season (four or however many season levels exist)
units_in: mu in abundance units; I_i dimensionless
units_out: slope of log10(I_i) on log10(mu), dimensionless
operation: Filters to strictly positive mu and I_i and draws a log-log scatter faceted by season with geom_smooth(method = lm); because faceting splits the data, this fits one regression per season on the log10 scale rather than one overall line. The inline comment says 'remove zeros' but the filter drops every non-positive value, not only zeros; on a strictly positive abundance index the two coincide, on a differenced or centred one they do not. The same operation on the same input recurs at lines 189-208, where the first line is again 'pop_inv %>%'; that repeat differs only in cosmetics (explicit formula = y ~ x, steelblue, theme_minimal), so it is the same node. The fitted slopes are drawn but never extracted, so nothing downstream consumes them.
settings: filter(mu > 0, I_i > 0); scale_x_log10 and scale_y_log10, so the fit is on log10 axes; method = lm, se = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE; facet_wrap(~ season), which is what makes the fit per-season
na_behavior: na.rm = TRUE suppresses the warning that would otherwise report dropped rows, so rows lost to non-finite values after log transformation vanish without a count. A season with too few points to fit produces no line and no message.

grain_in: one population: species x bay x season
grain_out: one fitted model: a single pooled slope with standard error, t and p
units_in: mu in abundance units; I_i dimensionless
units_out: slope m of log10(I_i) on log10(mu), dimensionless
operation: Fits and prints a single OLS of log10(I_i) on log10(mu) pooled over season, bay and species, on rows filtered to positive mu and I_i inside the call. This is a third, independently written filter of the same data (after line 167 and line 170) and is not tied to the df_taylor frame built later, so if one filter is edited the others do not follow. The output goes to the console only; the slope is not stored, so the number a reader sees here is not the number carried into anything else.
settings: log10 base; pooled, no season or bay term and no random effect for species, so the rows are treated as independent replicates; lm defaults (unweighted OLS, na.action = na.omit)
na_behavior: lm drops rows with NA silently under na.omit; the inline filter makes log10 of a non-positive value unreachable. If the filtered data had no rows or a constant log10(mu), lm would error rather than return, so failure is loud here rather than silent.

grain_in: one population: species x bay x season
grain_out: same grain, restricted to strictly positive finite mu and I_i, with variance and log columns added
units_in: mu in abundance units; I_i dimensionless
units_out: sigma2 in squared abundance units; log_mu, log_sigma2, log_I dimensionless
operation: Rebuilds the analysis frame: re-applies the finiteness test already applied at line 167, adds the positivity test, then back-computes the variance as sigma2 = mu^2 / I_i and takes log10 of mu, sigma2 and I_i; the mutate is absorbed because the log columns only carry the same three quantities into the model calls. The variance is not read from the source data, it is reconstructed from the invariability index, so whatever rounding or truncation I_i carries is inherited by sigma2, and log_sigma2 = 2*log_mu - log_I holds exactly by construction. That identity is why the two fits below are not independent evidence.
settings: filter(is.finite(mu), is.finite(I_i), mu > 0, I_i > 0); sigma2 = (mu^2)/I_i; log base 10 throughout
na_behavior: Rows failing any of the four tests are dropped without a count and without distinguishing which test removed them. A very small I_i can make sigma2 overflow to Inf; nothing rechecks finiteness after the mutate, so such a row reaches the fits and is then dropped by lm as NA/Inf handling dictates.

grain_in: one population: species x bay x season
grain_out: one scalar slope b plus its interval, t statistic and residual df
units_in: log10 abundance and log10 variance, dimensionless
operation: Fits the classic Taylor regression and extracts its slope, 95% interval, t statistic and residual degrees of freedom. The region's true first statement is line 226, 'fit_sigma <- lm(log_sigma2 ~ log_mu, data = df_taylor)', which cannot serve as an anchor because it carries a trailing comment, so the anchors start at the first comment-free line below it; lines 226-227 therefore sit outside every region for anchoring reasons only. The message at lines 239-240 formats b and its interval for the console and belongs to no node.
settings: OLS, unweighted, pooled over species, bay and season; confint at its default 0.95 level; no correction for repeated species across bays, so the interval treats every row as an independent observation
na_behavior: If the fit were rank deficient or log_mu constant, coef(fit_sigma)['log_mu'] would return NA and confint would return NA bounds; a rank-deficient fit and a mis-named coefficient both surface as the same NA, and nothing tests for it before the value is reported.

grain_in: one population: species x bay x season
grain_out: one scalar slope m plus its interval, t statistic and residual df
units_in: log10 abundance and log10 invariability, dimensionless
operation: Fits log_I on log_mu and extracts slope, 95% interval, t and residual df. The region's true first statement is line 227, 'fit_I     <- lm(log_I ~ log_mu, data = df_taylor)', which carries a trailing comment and so cannot be an anchor. Because log_I = 2*log_mu - log_sigma2 exactly by the construction in df_taylor, m = 2 - b algebraically and this fit re-expresses the previous one rather than testing it independently; the residual df and t statistic differ only through the intercept. Whether the two slopes are meant to be reported as separate results is a question the code cannot answer.
settings: OLS, unweighted, pooled; confint default 0.95 level; same rows as the b fit, since both use df_taylor
na_behavior: Same as the b node: a failed or rank-deficient fit yields NA slope and NA interval, indistinguishable from a coefficient-name mismatch, and is not tested before being printed.

start_anchor: p_a <- ggplot(df_taylor, aes(x = mu, y = sigma2, color = season)) +
grain_in: one population: species x bay x season
grain_out: one fitted line per season, drawn on log-log axes
units_in: mu in abundance units; sigma2 in squared abundance units
units_out: slope of log10(sigma2) on log10(mu) per season, dimensionless
operation: Draws panel (a), variance against mean on log-log axes. Because color = season sits in the global aes and the geom_smooth call respecifies only x and y, the smooth inherits the season grouping and fits one regression per season, not the single pooled line that the panel's role as the Taylor's law figure implies and that the pooled fit at line 226 computes. The legend is suppressed, so the per-season lines are drawn unlabelled and a reader is likely to take them for one relationship. Compare the saved version at line 263, which drops color from the global aes and therefore fits one line: the two panels are different operations, not restyled copies.
settings: method = lm, formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE, linewidth = 1; point alpha 0.25 size 1; scale_x_log10 and scale_y_log10 so the fit is on log10 axes; legend.position = none
na_behavior: No na.rm here, so non-finite values after log transformation are dropped by ggplot with a warning that is easy to miss in a long run; the count of dropped rows is not carried anywhere. A season with too few points silently produces no line.

start_anchor: p_a_bw <- ggplot(df_taylor, aes(x = mu, y = sigma2)) +
end_context: p_a_bw <- ggplot(df_taylor, aes(x = mu, y = sigma2)) +
grain_in: one population: species x bay x season
grain_out: one pooled fitted line drawn on log-log axes
units_in: mu in abundance units; sigma2 in squared abundance units
units_out: slope of log10(sigma2) on log10(mu), pooled, dimensionless
operation: Draws the black and white version of the same panel: season is mapped to grey only inside geom_point, so the global aes carries no colour and geom_smooth fits a single pooled regression across all seasons, matching the pooled b reported at line 229 and not matching the per-season panel above it. The greyscale, theme and linewidth statements are absorbed as styling. The ggsave at lines 292-297 writes this figure to results/Fig_6_taylor_loglog_8p5cm_600dpi.tif and is outside the region because it changes no quantity; the duplicated pt_mm assignment at lines 260-261 only supplies a line width.
settings: method = lm, formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE; single pooled fit; scale_color_grey(start 0.15, end 0.65); point alpha 0.35 size 0.1; linewidth = pt_mm (0.3527778 mm per point); base_size 7
na_behavior: No na.rm, so non-finite rows are dropped by ggplot with a warning and no retained count. If the fit failed, the panel would still be written to file by ggsave with the points and no line, and the saved figure would carry no indication of the failure.
